title: Crested Butte Winter
paragraphs: Skiers and snowboarders have a name for a day with no clouds at all: bluebird. Mid-February in Colorado handed me several! The week began in the mountains near Keystone. One day took me up onto a ridge above the trees, where the wind had scoured the crest down to dead grass and rippled the snow like sand. Beyond the valley, a long white range ran off to the horizon. In air that dry and cold, the far peaks looked sharp enough to cut yourself on.

Not far away, down in the spruce, stood a hand-built log lean-to, its poles lashed together, firewood stacked along one side and snow caught on the roof. When I came back three days later the sky had clouded over, and a gray jay was perched just outside the log frame. Gray jays stay in these forests all winter, gluing bits of food into the bark with their own sticky spit, and they've earned the nickname camp robber. This one looked like it was casing the place. Guard your lunch.

On the 17th the road to Crested Butte ran through the Arkansas Valley, and I pulled over more than once. Near Buena Vista the Collegiate Peaks rose out of the pastures with ribbons of cloud around their shoulders, the grass below tawny under a dusting of snow. Five of the range's fourteeners are named for colleges: Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Columbia and Oxford. That seems backwards to me. The mountains were teaching long before any of those schools opened.

By mid-afternoon I was snowboarding at Crested Butte Mountain Resort, where I spent the next couple of days. Spruce lined the runs and threw blue shadows across the snow, with bare aspens standing white among them. From one run I could see the valley floor far below and the long white skyline of the Elk Mountains beyond it. A pyramid of a peak, banded with layers of rock, caught the light from the side, and a snowboard standing upright in a drift supplied the only red in the frame. At Crested Butte it all came down to three colors: sky blue, snow white and spruce green.
